3.6 Credit Risk

Default risk and credit spreads

Section titled “Default risk and credit spreads”

The last two lessons assumed that bonds always pay as promised. US Treasuries are usually treated as free of default risk, but companies and local governments may fail to pay interest or principal. The risk that a borrower does not pay as promised is default risk. After a default, creditors usually do not lose everything: after the company is reorganized or liquidated, they recover part of what they are owed. The share of face value finally recovered is the recovery rate.

Consider a 1-year zero-coupon bond with face value 100. Let the probability of default be ppp, and let the creditor recover 100R100R100R after a default. The expected amount received at maturity is

E[CF]=(1−p)×100+p×100R=100 [1−p(1−R)]E[\text{CF}] = (1 - p) \times 100 + p \times 100R = 100\,[1 - p(1 - R)]E[CF]=(1−p)×100+p×100R=100[1−p(1−R)]

p(1−R)p(1 - R)p(1−R) is the expected loss rate. A bond’s yield to maturity is computed as if every payment is made as promised. The amount by which it exceeds the yield of a Treasury of the same maturity is the credit spread. If investors did not care about risk, the credit spread would only need to cover the expected loss, roughly p(1−R)p(1 - R)p(1−R).

Check C1
A corporate bond with default risk has a yield to maturity of 7%. An investor who buys it has an expected return of 7% as well.
Think: under what assumption is the yield to maturity computed? If there is some chance of default with only partial recovery, what happens to the money you can expect?

In practice, credit spreads are usually much larger than expected losses. Moody’s long-run statistics since 1920 show average annual default rates of about 0.1% for investment-grade corporate bonds and about 4% for speculative-grade bonds, and an average recovery rate of about 40% for senior unsecured bonds. Investment-grade spreads are often around 1 percentage point, far above an expected loss of about 0.06 percentage points. The main reasons are:

  • defaults are concentrated in recessions, when investors’ other assets (stocks, income from work) are also suffering, so investors demand a risk premium;
  • corporate bonds trade less actively than Treasuries and have wider bid-ask spreads, so investors demand compensation for liquidity;
  • in the US, Treasury interest is exempt from state and local income tax, while corporate bond interest is not.

Credit ratings

Section titled “Credit ratings”

Most investors cannot analyze every issuer themselves. Rating agencies such as S&P, Moody’s and Fitch grade the default risk of issuers or bonds; this grade is a credit rating. The grades of S&P and Fitch, from highest to lowest, are AAA, AA, A, BBB, BB, B, CCC and so on (with + or −); Moody’s uses Aaa, Aa, A, Baa, Ba, B, Caa and so on (with 1, 2 or 3). BBB− (Baa3) and above is investment grade; below that is speculative grade or high yield (informally, “junk”). The lower the rating, the higher the default rate and the wider the credit spread.

When using ratings, keep several points in mind:

  • A rating ranks the likelihood of default; it is not a forecast of prices. Market prices change every day, while ratings usually change slowly, often only after prices have already moved a lot.
  • Many institutional investors (for example, some insurers, pension funds and funds) have rules that allow them to hold only, or mainly, investment-grade bonds, so the line between investment grade and speculative grade matters a great deal.
  • Rating agencies earn most of their income from the issuers they rate.
Check C2
A company's bonds are downgraded from BBB− to BB+, while almost nothing new has happened to the business. Yet the bond price falls sharply. The main reason is:
BBB− to BB+ is one notch, and nothing new has happened to the business; the default probability does not suddenly double.
A rating ranks the likelihood of default; it is not a forecast of prices.
One company's downgrade does not change Treasury yields.

Treasuries, corporate bonds and municipal bonds

Section titled “Treasuries, corporate bonds and municipal bonds”

US bonds fall into three main groups by issuer:

  • Treasuries: issued by the federal government and usually treated as free of default risk; interest is subject to federal income tax but exempt from state and local income tax.
  • Corporate bonds: have default risk; interest is subject to federal and state income tax.
  • Municipal bond: a bond issued by a state or local government (or one of its agencies). Interest is usually exempt from federal income tax; for bonds issued in the investor’s own state, it is usually also exempt from that state’s income tax.

To compare tax-exempt and taxable bonds, look at after-tax returns. An investor with marginal tax rate ttt who holds a taxable bond yielding yyy keeps y(1−t)y(1 - t)y(1−t) after tax. To match the after-tax return of a tax-exempt municipal bond yielding ymy_mym​, a taxable bond must yield

yte=ym1−ty_{\text{te}} = \frac{y_m}{1 - t}yte​=1−tym​​

This is the tax-equivalent yield. In 2026, US federal marginal income tax rates range from 10% to 37% (IRS). The higher the tax rate, the more the exemption is worth, so the main buyers of municipal bonds are investors with high tax rates.

Check C3
Two investors both buy bonds in taxable accounts; one has a federal marginal tax rate of 12% and the other 37%. Who is more likely to gain from buying municipal bonds?
The benefit of municipal bonds comes from the tax exemption. With a lower tax rate a taxable bond loses less to tax; is the exemption worth more or less?
Both get the same return from the same municipal bond, but if they bought a taxable bond instead, they would keep different amounts after tax.
The comparison should use after-tax returns, not pre-tax yields.

Inflation-protected Treasuries

Section titled “Inflation-protected Treasuries”

Ordinary Treasuries pay fixed nominal amounts, so the higher the inflation, the lower their real value. The principal of TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) is adjusted by the consumer price index (CPI): inflation raises the principal in the same proportion, and coupons are paid at a fixed coupon rate on the adjusted principal. At maturity, if the adjusted principal is below the original face value, the original face value is repaid. So the yield of TIPS is a real yield (real interest rate).

Let the yield of a nominal Treasury be yyy and the real yield of a TIPS of the same maturity be yry_ryr​. If average inflation is π\piπ, the real return of the nominal Treasury is 1+y1+π−1\frac{1 + y}{1 + \pi} - 11+π1+y​−1. The inflation rate at which the two are equal is breakeven inflation:

1+πbe=1+y1+yr,πbe≈y−yr1 + \pi_{\text{be}} = \frac{1 + y}{1 + y_r}, \qquad \pi_{\text{be}} \approx y - y_r1+πbe​=1+yr​1+y​,πbe​≈y−yr​

If inflation turns out above it, TIPS do better; if below, the nominal Treasury does better.

Check C4
In Figure 4-1, the nominal Treasury yields 4.2% and TIPS yield 1.9% real. If inflation averages 4% over the next 10 years, which bond has the higher real value after 10 years?
The nominal yield is higher because it compensates for expected inflation. Compare returns after actual inflation.
They are equal only if inflation exactly equals breakeven inflation. Roughly what is breakeven inflation here?
Both are held to maturity, so their real values after 10 years depend only on the yields and actual inflation, not on future interest rates.

Although the principal adjustment of TIPS is received only at maturity, in the US it is taxed as interest income every year, so TIPS are better held in accounts that defer tax, such as retirement accounts (Exercises Question 4).

Bond funds and individual bonds

Section titled “Bond funds and individual bonds”

Individual investors can buy individual bonds or bond funds. The main differences are:

  • An individual bond has a maturity date; held to maturity (without default), it pays a known nominal amount. A bond fund keeps buying new bonds and selling bonds near maturity; it has no maturity date, and its duration stays roughly constant.
  • A fund holds hundreds or even thousands of bonds and so diversifies away the default risk of single issuers; buying corporate bonds yourself, such diversification is hard to achieve.
  • Trading individual corporate and municipal bonds is usually costly (wide bid-ask spreads); a fund’s size keeps its trading costs low, but it charges a management fee.

A common claim is: “An individual bond held to maturity cannot lose money, while a fund loses when rates rise.” Is this right? Exercises Question 5 analyzes this question using 3.4 Interest Rate Risk.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Default risk is described by the probability of default ppp and the recovery rate RRR; the expected loss rate is p(1−R)p(1 - R)p(1−R). Credit spreads also include a risk premium, compensation for liquidity and tax differences, so they are usually larger than expected losses.
  • Credit ratings rank default risk; BBB− (Baa3) and above is investment grade. Ratings change slowly, and agencies are paid by issuers.
  • Municipal bond interest is usually exempt from federal income tax; the tax-equivalent yield is yte=ym1−ty_{\text{te}} = \frac{y_m}{1 - t}yte​=1−tym​​.
  • The principal of TIPS is adjusted by the CPI and their yield is a real yield; breakeven inflation is πbe≈y−yr\pi_{\text{be}} \approx y - y_rπbe​≈y−yr​.
  • Bond funds diversify default risk and have low trading costs, but have no maturity date, and their duration stays roughly constant.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
A high-yield bond fund has a yield to maturity of 7.5%, while Treasuries of the same maturity yield 4.3%. Assume the fund's bonds default at 4% a year with a recovery rate of 40%.
(a) Roughly what is the fund's expected annual return? How much above Treasuries is it?
(b) An investor wants to replace the Treasuries in his portfolio with this fund because it "yields much more". Using when defaults happen (2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices), explain the problem with this.
Question 2
(a) A bond has a 2% chance of default each year (independent across years). What is the probability that it defaults within 5 years?
(b) Many such loans are pooled and split into layers of securities by the order in which they absorb losses: the first layer absorbs the first 10% of losses, and the "senior layer" above it loses only if losses exceed 10%. If defaults on the loans were independent, the senior layer would almost never lose. Why can such a senior layer be far more dangerous than its rating suggests when defaults are highly correlated (for example, in a nationwide fall in house prices)?
Question 3
An investor has a federal marginal tax rate of 37% and a state income tax rate of 9.3% (simplification: add the two rates). The choices are an in-state municipal bond at 3.2%, a Treasury at 4.2% and a corporate bond at 4.9%, with similar maturities.
(a) In a taxable account, what is the after-tax yield of each? Which should he choose?
(b) If the same investor buys bonds in a tax-deferred retirement account, how does the choice change? Use this to explain why it matters which account an asset is held in.
Question 4
You buy TIPS with face value 1000 and a real coupon rate of 1.5% (simplified to one payment a year). In the first year the CPI rises 3%.
(a) What are the adjusted principal at year end and the coupon received that year? In the US, how much interest income is taxable that year? Is this more or less than the cash received?
(b) Why are TIPS better held in tax-deferred accounts? If cumulative deflation before maturity pushes the adjusted principal below 1000, how much is paid at maturity?
Question 5
An investor will need money in 5 years. He can buy a Treasury maturing in 5 years and hold it to maturity, or buy a Treasury fund with a modified duration of 4.8 and a Macaulay duration of about 5 years. Right after he buys, rates of all maturities rise by 2 percentage points.
(a) Roughly how much does the fund's value change? What about the market value of the individual Treasury?
(b) Is the claim "an individual bond held to maturity cannot lose money" right? Using 3.4 Interest Rate Risk, explain roughly how the two approaches end up after 5 years.
